The PMC copy was blocked by a browser check and was not read.

title: Evaluating Reasoning Faithfulness in Medical Vision-Language Models using Multimodal Perturbations
journal: Proceedings of the Fifth Machine Learning for Health Symposium (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Proposes a perturbation test of chain-of-thought explanations in chest radiograph VQA: text and image cues are deliberately injected or altered and the explanation is scored on clinical fidelity, causal attribution (does it acknowledge what actually changed the answer) and confidence calibration. Across six vision-language models, answer accuracy and explanation quality diverged, mentioning an injected cue did not mean the reasoning was grounded in it, and text cues moved explanations more than image cues; proprietary models attributed far more often than open-source ones (25.0% vs 1.4%). An automated evaluator agreed with radiologists within the inter-radiologist range in a 4-reader study (Kendall tau-b 0.670 for attribution, 0.387 for fidelity, 0.091 for confidence tone). Implication: fluent step-by-step rationales from these models are often not faithful to how the answer was reached.
use_for: Direct evidence that natural-language rationales from medical vision-language models can be unfaithful; method for testing faithfulness
verified_how: PMLR proceedings page (title, authors, volume, pages, abstract) + arXiv abstract page
flags: Chest radiograph VQA, not CT; included as the faithfulness reference. ML4H 2025 symposium, PMLR volume dated 2026 (published 5 May 2026); online_date is the arXiv v1 date (arXiv:2510.11196). No DOI. Small reader study (n=4), and the confidence-tone axis had weak agreement.

title: The effect of medical explanations from large language models on diagnostic accuracy in radiology
key_finding: A randomised between-subjects vignette experiment with 101 US radiologists (2,020 free-text diagnoses on 20 published image-challenge cases with CT or MRI) compared no LLM support against three GPT-4 output formats: diagnosis only, a five-item differential, and a chain-of-thought explanation. Chain-of-thought output gave the highest accuracy, 12.2 points above control (P = 0.001), 7.2 above diagnosis-only and 9.7 above the differential format, and the effect held across case difficulty and radiologist specialisation. Implication: the format of a text explanation changes clinician accuracy, and stepwise reasoning helped readers spot wrong LLM answers in this setting.
use_for: Evidence that natural-language reasoning explanations can help radiologists; counterpoint to overreliance findings
verified_how: Nature (npj Digital Medicine) landing page (abstract, methods, volume, article number) + Crossref record (8 authors)
flags: Text-only LLM given case descriptions (not a vision model reading the scan); online vignette study with curated challenge cases, CT or MRI, not chest-specific. The abstract states gains as percent while the results describe percentage points. The medRxiv preprint (10.1101/2025.03.04.25323357) had a slightly different title ('...on diagnostic decisions in radiology').

title: Evaluating Explainability: A Framework for Systematic Assessment of Explainable AI Features in Medical Imaging
key_finding: Authors from the US FDA device centre propose a staged framework for testing heatmap-type explanations of imaging AI on four criteria: consistency (stability under small input changes, scored with SSIM, MSE or IoU), plausibility (overlap with lesion ground truth), fidelity (model-parameter randomisation and incremental deletion) and usefulness (human reader studies), plus an 'explainability card' for reporting. In a case study with 150 synthetic mammograms (M-SYNTH) and a Faster R-CNN detector, Ablation-CAM scored higher than Eigen-CAM on plausibility and fidelity, while both maps fluctuated under dose and rotation changes that left detection accuracy stable. Usefulness was not tested, no acceptance thresholds are set, and exact metric values are given only in figures.
use_for: 1 - regulator-authored framework naming the four evaluation axes (consistency, plausibility, fidelity, usefulness) and a reporting card; supports the argument that faithfulness and plausibility must be tested separately and before reader studies
verified_how: MDPI article page (abstract and full text read)
flags: Case study uses synthetic mammography only, not chest CT. Numeric results appear only in figures, so no headline number is recorded. Affiliations are given for the group as a whole on the page.

title: Evaluating the robustness of explainable AI in medical image recognition under natural and adversarial data corruption
key_finding: Benchmarks the stability of ten post-hoc explanation methods (eight for CNNs including Integrated Gradients, SmoothGrad, Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++; AttnLRP and LibraGrad for transformers) on eight classifiers across three MedMNIST sets (dermatoscopy, paediatric chest radiographs with 5,856 images, retinal OCT), under natural corruptions (contrast reduction, JPEG compression, speckle noise) and an adversarial attack that alters the explanation while keeping the predicted class. Stability is scored with L2 distance, SSIM and a new spatial metric (Convolution Density Agreement); 160 configurations per data set. Many methods changed under imperceptible perturbations and no method was best on every metric: SmoothGrad was most stable against the attack and Grad-CAM++ against natural noise for CNNs.
use_for: 1 (also 2) - robustness/stability of saliency maps as a separate evaluation axis, with a head-to-head comparison of ten attribution methods that includes chest radiographs
verified_how: Springer article page (abstract and full text read) + Crossref record for the author list
flags: Springer page truncates the byline with an ellipsis; the six-author list is taken from Crossref. Table values were not visible in the fetched page, so no numeric scores are quoted. Images are 224x224 MedMNIST benchmarks, not clinical-resolution CT.

title: Faithful Faithfulness Evaluations: Challenges & Pitfalls Learned from a Breast MRI Case Study
key_finding: Compares seven saliency methods (last-layer attention, attention rollout, Grad-SAM, gradient attention rollout, GMAR, Grad-CAM, HiResCAM) for a transformer classifier of 3D breast MRI (ODELIA challenge data, 1,022 unilateral breast volumes, 116 in the test set) using deletion and insertion curves summarised as area under the confidence curve. Method rankings changed with the masking strategy (black, white, minimum intensity, attention masking); with fixed-intensity masking most methods were close to random ordering. Grad-CAM and gradient attention rollout were the strongest class-specific methods (deletion AUCC 0.336 each versus 0.512 for random), but their order depended on the protocol, and the advantage shrank when class-agnostic variants were compared.
use_for: 2 (also 1) - disagreement between saliency methods on volumetric MRI and the dependence of deletion/insertion rankings on how regions are removed; caution for any faithfulness table reported in chest CT studies
verified_how: alphaXiv full text of arXiv:2609.25978v1
flags: PREPRINT, not peer reviewed; no venue stated. Breast MRI, single model with moderate accuracy (macro AUROC 0.73). The classifier processes volumes slice-wise. No published version found by web search on 2026-10-10.

title: Decision processes in 3D structural MRI schizophrenia classification evaluated with saliency maps
key_finding: Trained seven 3D deep learning architectures (two from scratch, five pretrained) to separate schizophrenia from controls on T1-weighted MRI of 192 adults (101 patients, 91 controls; MCIC collection) and examined each with Grad-CAM. Plausibility was judged visually and with two quantitative measures: share of saliency mass inside the brain, and centre-of-mass deviation and spread. All models reached similar accuracy (above 70%, AUC above 0.75, no significant differences), yet only two of the seven (BrainID and ResNet18) based their decisions on plausible brain structure.
use_for: 2 (also 4) - volumetric example where equal accuracy hides different decision bases: saliency maps exposed five of seven 3D models as relying on implausible regions
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract and full text read)
flags: Brain MRI, not chest imaging. Only Grad-CAM was used, so this compares models rather than explanation methods. Small single-collection sample without lesion-level ground truth.

title: Evaluating cognitive biases in AI-assisted mammography interpretation: a simulation reader study of explainable AI across radiologist experience levels
key_finding: Single-centre, fully crossed simulation study: six breast radiologists of three experience levels read 200 mammograms unaided, with AI, and with AI plus saliency heatmaps; the AI's BI-RADS-like recommendation was deliberately shifted by one category in 30% of examinations. Without heatmaps, automation bias occurred in 65/180 (36.1%) and anchoring-related revision in 61/180 (33.9%) manipulated readings; with heatmaps these fell to 32/180 (17.8%) and 31/180 (17.2%) (adjusted odds ratios 0.56 and 0.61, both p<0.001). On unmanipulated cases accuracy rose from 86.2% unaided to 90.1% with AI plus heatmaps; less experienced readers were most affected and the bias was reduced but not removed.
use_for: 3 - experimental evidence that heatmap explanations can roughly halve, but not eliminate, automation and anchoring bias when the AI is wrong
verified_how: Springer article page (abstract read)
flags: Mammography, six readers, one centre, enriched case mix and an artificially high AI error rate. The 180-reading denominator per condition is as reported in the abstract and was not reconciled with 200 cases x 6 readers x 30% from the full text.

title: Automation Bias in Action: Eye Tracking of Humans Reading Screening Mammograms with and without AI Prompts
key_finding: Retrospective paired multireader study with eye tracking: 10 readers from the UK breast screening programme read 60 two-view screening mammograms unaided and, six weeks later, with a commercial AI tool that displayed region prompts (26 true-positive, 14 false-negative, 14 false-positive, 6 true-negative AI outputs). For cancers the AI missed, median reader sensitivity fell from 71% unaided to 39% with AI (P=.002); for false-positive AI cases median specificity rose from 21% to 39% (P=.004). Reading time rose with the number of prompts (median 25 s with none to 34 s with four or more) and fixation rate on missed cancers was lower with AI.
use_for: 3 - direct measurement of automation bias and altered visual search from incorrect localisation prompts; reading-time cost of on-image AI marks
verified_how: RSNA article page (abstract read)
flags: Mammography; the 'explanation' here is a localisation prompt with a score, not a saliency map. Article e-number not shown on the page (pages left null). Study funded by the AI vendor (Lunit), stated as not involved in the article.

title: Dermatologist-like explainable AI enhances melanoma diagnosis accuracy: eye-tracking study
key_finding: Reader study with eye tracking in which 76 dermatologists each diagnosed 16 dermoscopic images of melanomas and naevi, first with a plain AI prediction and then with an explainable AI giving domain-specific explanations. Mean balanced accuracy rose from 79.9% with AI to 82.7% with explainable AI (gain 2.8 percentage points, P=0.013). Disagreement with the classifier and difficult lesions were associated with more fixations, read by the authors as higher cognitive load; the accuracy gain was unrelated to years of experience and trust was not measured in this study.
use_for: 3 - non-radiology comparator showing a small but significant accuracy gain from concept-style explanations over AI alone, with gaze data on cognitive load
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract and results read) + Crossref record for the author list
flags: Dermoscopy, not radiology. Byline has 20 named authors, the Reader Study Consortium and the senior author; Crossref also lists about 80 consortium members as individual authors, which are not reproduced here. Fixed order (AI first, then explainable AI) rather than randomised arms; the gain was significant in the webcam cohort (n=51) but not in the device-based cohort (n=25).

title: Mask of Truth: Model Sensitivity to Unexpected Regions of Medical Images
journal: Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine
key_finding: Tests for shortcut learning by training DenseNet-121 classifiers on chest radiographs with the lungs removed or kept (PadChest, 93,203 images after filtering, five findings; external test on 22,004 ChestX-ray14 images) and on fundus images (Chaksu). Chest models stayed well above chance with the lungs masked out by a bounding box (effusion AUC 0.85-0.93, pneumonia at least 0.74) and above metadata-only baselines, while lung-only images gave AUCs near 0.5 for several findings. SHAP maps pointed to a pacemaker for cardiomegaly and to peripheral image areas; a radiology resident identified only 2 of 35 present conditions on the masked images, and external performance was far lower than internal.
use_for: 4 - masking experiment plus SHAP showing chest radiograph classifiers can perform without the clinically relevant region; also notes that local attribution maps can miss global shortcuts
verified_how: Springer article page (abstract and full text read) + Crossref record
flags: Chest radiographs and fundus, not CT. Online first 20 May 2025; assigned to volume 39 issue 1 (February 2026). Springer page truncated the byline; the five-author list is from Crossref. Crossref short title is recorded as shown.

title: Explainable AI reveals Clever Hans effects in unsupervised learning models
key_finding: Uses explanation methods to show that unsupervised representation-learning and anomaly-detection models, including foundation models, often predict correctly for the wrong reasons. In the medical example a COVID-19 detector built on PubMedCLIP features (2,597 NIH CXR8 radiographs plus 535 images from a public COVID-19 collection) reached 87.5% class-balanced accuracy overall but only 81.7% with a 51% false-positive rate on the COVID-source subset; BiLRP explanations traced this to text-like annotations on the images. The authors attribute the effect largely to inductive biases of the unsupervised learner and report that targeted mitigation improved robustness.
use_for: 4 - Clever Hans effect inherited from a pretrained medical foundation model and exposed by explanations in a chest radiograph task; relevant to foundation-model-based chest CT pipelines
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract and results read) + Crossref record for the author list
flags: The chest radiograph experiment is one of several use cases; most of the paper is general machine learning. Chest radiographs, not CT.

title: Uncertainty-Driven Training for Three-Dimensional Calibrated Lung Nodule Classification
journal: Artificial Neural Networks and Machine Learning - ICANN 2026 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 17092)
key_finding: Proposes a training scheme for 3D CT lung nodule classifiers in which validation-set uncertainty estimates reweight the loss towards unreliable classes, comparing Monte Carlo dropout with evidential deep learning on five backbones (ResNet, DenseNet, EfficientNet, ViT, Swin) using LIDC-IDRI and NoduleMNIST3D. Classification performance stayed similar to standard training while expected calibration error fell by up to 65% on LIDC-IDRI; gains were more consistent for convolutional than transformer backbones, evidential learning degraded on ViT, and simple post-hoc temperature scaling was highly effective in every configuration.
use_for: 5 - chest CT evidence that nodule classifiers are miscalibrated by default and that calibration (expected calibration error) should be reported alongside accuracy; temperature scaling as a strong baseline
verified_how: Springer chapter page (abstract; full text behind preview) + arXiv abstract page 2609.20905
flags: Conference paper (ICANN 2026). Springer shows first online 14 September 2026 but a 2027 copyright/citation year; year is recorded as 2027 with the 2026 online date, so it counts as 2026 under the online-first rule. Only the abstract was read, which gives a single number (up to 65% ECE reduction); absolute ECE values and nodule counts are not recorded. No explanation method or reader study is involved.

title: Human-AI Collaboration in Radiology: The Blind Spots
key_finding: Special report (narrative synthesis, no new data) arguing that radiology AI research has concentrated on stand-alone algorithm performance while the human-AI interaction that determines clinical value is poorly understood. It sets out three under-recognised determinants: cognitive psychology (automation bias, how AI uncertainty is framed, AI-induced skill decay), interface and user-experience design (timing, prominence and documentation of AI findings), and algorithmic conformity driven by medicolegal, transparency and organisational pressure; research directions are proposed for each.
use_for: 5 (also 3) - peer-reviewed synthesis linking how AI output and uncertainty are presented to automation bias and reliance; frames explanation and confidence display as interface-design questions
verified_how: RSNA article page (abstract read; full text paywalled)
flags: Narrative special report, not a systematic review; only the abstract was read. Article e-number not shown on the page (pages left null). Not specific to chest CT.

title: Low-dose CT for lung cancer screening in a high-risk population (SUMMIT): a prospective, longitudinal cohort study
key_finding: Prospective London cohort (329 primary care practices) of 12,773 high-risk people aged 55-77 screened with low-dose CT; this report covers the baseline round. Lung cancer was diagnosed in 261 participants (2.0%), 79.3% at stage I or II and 77.0% treated by surgical resection; 12-month episode sensitivity was 97.0% and specificity 95.2% (false-positive rate 4.8%), with 11.6% of surgical resections benign. The authors conclude that large-scale LDCT screening can be delivered effectively to an ethnically and socioeconomically diverse population.
use_for: Introduction: recent prospective evidence that LDCT lung cancer screening works at scale (drives chest CT volume)
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + UCL Discovery repository record (abstract)
flags: Author list: Crossref gives 139 author entries (named writing group followed by SUMMIT consortium members, with repeats); the 36 names listed here are the first block before names start repeating and are taken to be the byline, published on behalf of the SUMMIT consortium - check against the journal PDF. Crossref shows an erratum (DOI 10.1016/S1470-2045(25)00204-9, May 2025) whose content I did not read. Online-first date not shown. Lancet website could not be opened. Funded by GRAIL.

title: Feasibility of AI as first reader in the 4-IN-THE-LUNG-RUN lung cancer screening trial: impact on negative-misclassifications and clinical referral rate
key_finding: On 3,678 baseline low-dose CT scans from the 4-IN-THE-LUNG-RUN trial, a commercial AI system (AVIEW-LCS) and radiologists read independently against an expert-panel reference. AI produced 31 negative misclassifications (0.8%) versus 407 (11.1%) for radiologists; used as first reader, AI would have missed 3 of 102 referrals (2.9%) compared with 12 of 102 (11.8%) for radiologists. The authors conclude AI is a feasible first reader to rule out negative baseline scans.
use_for: Clinical context: AI as an autonomous or first reader in CT screening, which raises the stakes for explanation and oversight
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + Erasmus University repository record (abstract)
flags: Crossref lists a corrigendum (DOI 10.1016/j.ejca.2025.115294, Eur J Cancer vol 218, March 2025); I could not read what it corrects, so re-check the numbers against the corrected version. ScienceDirect page not opened. Issue number not assigned (volume 216, article 115214).

title: Projected US Imaging Utilization, 2025 to 2055
journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
key_finding: Using 2018-2022 claims (Medicare fee-for-service 5% sample plus the Inovalon database; 348,214,053 person-years), the authors project US imaging use to 2055. If current per-person use simply persists, 2055 utilisation is 16.9% to 26.9% above 2023 levels depending on modality; if recent trends continue to 2030 the range is 5.6% lower to 45.2% higher. Population growth explains 73-88% of the increase and ageing 12-27%.
use_for: Introduction: growth in imaging demand and radiologist workload as a driver for AI assistance
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + Ochsner institutional repository record (abstract)
flags: Covers all imaging modalities in the US, not chest CT specifically. Journal abbreviation 'J Am Coll Radiol' seen on the repository page (Crossref short title is the full name). Online-first date not shown. ScienceDirect page not opened.

title: External Test of a Deep Learning Algorithm for Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy Risk Stratification Using European Screening Data
key_finding: A nodule malignancy-risk deep learning model trained on NLST was tested retrospectively on pooled baseline scans from three European screening trials (DLCST, MILD, NELSON): 4,146 participants, 7,614 benign and 180 malignant nodules. AUCs were 0.98, 0.96 and 0.94 for cancers diagnosed within 1 year, 2 years and over the whole screening period, at least matching the PanCan model; for indeterminate 5-15 mm nodules, at 100% sensitivity for 1-year cancers, the model labelled 68.1% of benign cases low risk versus 47.4% for PanCan (a 39.4% relative reduction in false positives). On a size-matched subset the AUC was 0.79 versus 0.60.
use_for: Performance of deep learning on chest CT: large multi-trial external validation (2025)
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page + UMC Utrecht repository record (abstract)
flags: Byline ends 'for the NELSON-POP consortium'; Crossref additionally lists the consortium members as authors (not included here). Retrospective design.

title: External Testing of a Deep Learning Model for Lung Cancer Risk from Low-Dose Chest CT
key_finding: The open-source Sybil lung-cancer-risk model was tested on 18,057 adults aged 50-80 from one Asian health-checkup centre (92 cancers over 6 years). Overall AUC was 0.91 for 1-year and 0.74 for 6-year risk; in heavy smokers the 1-year AUC for visible cancers was 0.94 and the 6-year AUC for future cancers 0.70, but in never- or light-smokers the AUC for future cancers fell to 0.56 (visible cancers 0.89). The model therefore transfers poorly to a population outside its training distribution for the task of predicting future cancer.
use_for: Generalisation limits of chest CT deep learning across populations (motivates transparency about where a model can be trusted)
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page + Jeonbuk National University repository record (abstract)
flags: Single-centre retrospective external test; the generalisation gap is across population/smoking status rather than across scanners.

title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
key_finding: Consensus guideline from 117 experts in 50 countries setting out 30 best practices under six principles: fairness, universality, traceability, usability, robustness and explainability. Explainability has two recommendations: decide with end users and domain experts whether explanations are needed and define their goal, approach and limitations; and evaluate explanations both computationally for correctness and with end users for their effect on satisfaction, confidence and clinical performance. Traceability has six (risk management file, documentation, continuous quality control with calibrated uncertainty, periodic auditing and updating, AI logging, and governance with defined accountability).
use_for: Guidelines and regulation: current international consensus on what explainability and traceability require of clinical AI
verified_how: Crossref record + BMJ landing page (summary and recommendations) + BMJ correction notice
flags: A correction (BMJ 2025;388:r340, 17 Feb 2025) only fixes the spelling of a consortium member's name. The 49 named authors publish with the FUTURE-AI Consortium as a group; the exact wording of the group byline was not checked. Crossref gives no issue number.

title: Guiding AI in radiology: ESR's recommendations for effective implementation of the European AI Act
key_finding: ESR AI Working Group statement on how the EU AI Act applies to imaging. Medical-device AI falls in the high-risk class; Article 13 obliges providers to give deployers clear instructions on intended purpose, performance, limitations and oversight measures, for which the ESR recommends model cards; Article 14 requires trained human oversight, with warnings about automation bias and deskilling; and under Article 26 any radiologist or department using AI clinically is a deployer who must follow instructions, supervise, monitor, keep logs and inform patients. The statement notes that methods and standards for transparency and explainability are still under development and asks the European Commission for sector-specific implementation guidance.
use_for: Regulation: EU AI Act transparency and human-oversight duties as read by European radiology
verified_how: Springer landing page (full statement) + Crossref record
flags: Article type is a society statement; the European Society of Radiology is listed as a group author.

title: On the practical, ethical, and legal necessity of clinical Artificial Intelligence explainability: an examination of key arguments
journal: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
key_finding: Systematized review of the arguments for and against requiring explainability in clinical AI. The authors conclude that fully autonomous black-box algorithms are persuasively ruled out on fundamental-rights and justice grounds, but that the published arguments do not establish a general explainability requirement for clinician-in-the-loop use, because lack of explanation does not by itself undermine clinicians' due diligence. They hold that trust should rest on transparency of development and sound clinical decision-making.
use_for: Debate on whether explainability should be a requirement for clinical AI (the 'against a blanket requirement' position)
verified_how: Springer landing page (abstract and conclusions) + Crossref record
flags: General clinical AI, not imaging-specific. The Springer page metadata listed only Veerapen but the byline and Crossref show both authors.

title: Global cancer statistics 2022: GLOBOCAN estimates of incidence and mortality worldwide for 36 cancers in 185 countries
journal: CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians
key_finding: IARC GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates give close to 20 million new cancer cases and 9.7 million cancer deaths worldwide in 2022. Lung cancer was the most frequently diagnosed cancer (almost 2.5 million new cases, 12.4% of all cancers) and the leading cause of cancer death (about 1.8 million deaths, 18.7% of cancer deaths), ahead of female breast (11.6% of cases) and colorectal cancer (9.6% of cases; 9.3% of deaths). New cases are projected to reach 35 million by 2050 on demographic change alone.
use_for: Introduction: global lung cancer burden as the clinical motivation for chest CT AI
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata + abstract field)
flags: Published 2024 (allowed by task as the latest GLOBOCAN statistics paper). Publisher (Wiley) page not opened; numbers taken from the abstract deposited in Crossref.

title: PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR): Checklist and Explanation
key_finding: Abstract not read (the publisher page did not render it). From the publisher page structure and the official PRISMA site: this is the reporting guideline for scoping reviews, with 20 essential and 2 optional reporting items; the two optional items concern critical appraisal of the sources of evidence, and five items of the original PRISMA list are marked not applicable. It was developed through an expert panel, Delphi survey rounds and an in-person meeting.

verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + ACP publisher page (headings and item structure) + PRISMA statement website (item counts) + EQUATOR Network entry

The abstract text itself was not visible on any page I could open, so the item counts come from prisma-statement.org and the item structure from the article's explanation section; the size of the expert panel was not seen and is not stated here. PubMed and PMC were blocked by a browser check.

title: Fleischner Society: Glossary of Terms for Thoracic Imaging
key_finding: Fourth edition of the Fleischner Society consensus glossary, replacing the 1984, 1996 and 2008 versions. Terms were revised because some are new, some obsolete and others inconsistently used; related terms are grouped under thematic headings, signs and eponyms are reduced in favour of descriptive terms, each term is labelled as anatomy, physiology or pathology, and many more radiograph and CT images are included, with recommended usage given for controversial terms. Its stated aims include standardised communication, structured reporting and database searching.
use_for: Imaging vocabulary: authoritative term set a concept-based explanation layer for chest CT could draw on
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page (abstract and introduction)
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document, allowed by task). The abstract gives no count of terms. Online-first date not shown (issue date February 2024).

title: The Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) and Image Database Resource Initiative (IDRI): A Completed Reference Database of Lung Nodules on CT Scans
key_finding: Describes the public LIDC-IDRI database of 1,018 thoracic CT cases assembled by seven academic centres and eight imaging companies. Each scan was annotated by four experienced thoracic radiologists in two phases (blinded read, then unblinded review of all four sets of marks) using three categories: nodule 3 mm or larger, nodule smaller than 3 mm, and non-nodule 3 mm or larger. In total 7,371 lesions were marked as a nodule by at least one radiologist, 2,669 of them in the 3 mm-or-larger nodule category by at least one reader.
use_for: Imaging vocabulary and data: the reference dataset whose radiologist-rated nodule attributes underlie most concept-based chest CT XAI work
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata + abstract) + The Cancer Imaging Archive collection page (citation and dataset description)
flags: Essential original (2011). The three marking categories are taken from the TCIA collection page; the Crossref abstract supplied the counts. TCIA lists 1,010 subjects for what the paper describes as 1,018 cases. TCIA's citation omits the last author (Clarke LP) and has minor spelling variants; the Crossref spellings are used here. Wiley publisher page not opened.

title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
key_finding: Introduces Grad-CAM, which weights the feature maps of the last convolutional layer by the gradients of a target class score to give a coarse heat map of the image regions behind a prediction. The method needs no architectural change, applies to classification, captioning and visual question answering networks, and is reported to help users judge model reliability.
use_for: Essential original: definition of Grad-CAM
verified_how: Springer landing page + Crossref record
flags: Pre-2025 essential original (journal version of the ICCV 2017 paper).

title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
journal: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NIPS 2017)
key_finding: Proposes SHAP, a framework that assigns each input feature an importance value for an individual prediction. It shows that a class of additive feature-importance measures has a unique solution with desirable properties and that this class covers six earlier explanation methods.
use_for: Essential original: definition of SHAP
verified_how: NeurIPS proceedings abstract page
flags: Pre-2025 essential original. Page numbers and editors are not shown on the proceedings page; no DOI.

title: Concept Bottleneck Models
journal: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Introduces the concept bottleneck model: a network first predicts human-specified concepts that are labelled at training time and then predicts the target from those concepts alone, so that a user can edit concept values at test time and see the prediction change. On x-ray grading of arthritis severity (clinical concepts) and bird identification (attribute concepts) the models were competitive with end-to-end networks, and correcting wrong concept predictions at test time improved accuracy substantially.
use_for: original definition of CBMs and test-time concept intervention
verified_how: PMLR proceedings page
flags: Essential original (pre-2025). No DOI (PMLR). The proceedings abstract does not name the datasets.

title: Addressing Leakage in Concept Bottleneck Models
journal: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022)
key_finding: Explains that passing the concept predictor's output probabilities to the label predictor improves label accuracy but lets extra, non-concept information leak through, which lowers concept accuracy and makes test-time interventions less effective. It attributes the trade-off to an insufficient concept set and an inexpressive concept predictor, and with corresponding modifications obtains models that match the accuracy of leaky CBMs while greatly improving concept accuracy and intervention accuracy.
use_for: definition and mitigation of concept leakage
verified_how: NeurIPS proceedings page (Main Conference Track) + NeurIPS virtual poster page
flags: Essential original (pre-2025). Page range was reported from the proceedings page's citation metadata rather than printed on the visible page; the DOI shown is the Curran Associates proceedings DOI.

title: This Looks Like That: Deep Learning for Interpretable Image Recognition
journal: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019)
key_finding: Introduces the prototypical part network (ProtoPNet), which classifies an image by finding parts that resemble learned class prototypes and summing that evidence, trained with image-level labels only. On CUB-200-2011 birds and Stanford Cars it reached accuracy close to non-interpretable counterparts, and ensembles of ProtoPNets matched some of the best deep models. Natural images only; no medical data and no human evaluation of the prototypes are described in the abstract.
use_for: (1) prototype-based models: essential original for the ProtoPNet family
verified_how: NeurIPS proceedings abstract page (title, authors, volume, year, abstract)
flags: Essential original (2019). Page numbers and DOI not shown on the page opened.

title: Stop explaining black box machine learning models for high stakes decisions and use interpretable models instead
key_finding: Perspective arguing that post hoc explanation of black-box models in high-stakes settings such as healthcare and criminal justice can entrench bad practice, and that models should instead be designed to be interpretable from the start. It distinguishes explaining a black box from using an inherently interpretable model, lists reasons to avoid the former and challenges for the latter, and gives examples from criminal justice, healthcare and computer vision.

title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
journal: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31 (NeurIPS 2018)
key_finding: Introduces randomisation tests for saliency methods: an explanation should change when the trained model's parameters or the training labels are randomised. Several popular methods produced maps that were largely independent of both the model and the data-generating process, behaving like edge detectors, so visual appeal alone is a misleading criterion; theory for a linear model and a one-layer convolutional network supports the experiments.

title: Assessing the Trustworthiness of Saliency Maps for Localizing Abnormalities in Medical Imaging
key_finding: Evaluated eight saliency methods (gradient, SmoothGrad, integrated gradients, smooth integrated gradients, Grad-CAM, XRAI, guided backpropagation, guided Grad-CAM) on chest radiograph classifiers using the SIIM-ACR pneumothorax set (10,675 images) and the RSNA pneumonia set (14,863 images), against four criteria: localisation utility, sensitivity to weight randomisation, repeatability and reproducibility, scored with AUPRC and SSIM. Every method failed at least one criterion and all localised worse than dedicated networks (AUPRC 0.024-0.224 versus 0.404 for U-Net in segmentation; 0.160-0.519 versus 0.596 for RetinaNet in detection).
